passage: Every evening for two months, Joseph practised his badminton serve against the wall of their Mumbai building. The watchman got used to the tok-tok sound. At the colony tournament he reached the final against Zubin, who was a year older. Joseph's serves were clean, but Zubin was quicker at the net and won by three points. Joseph's throat felt tight. He walked to the net and shook Zubin's hand. "Your smashes are brilliant." Zubin grinned. "Your serve was tough to return. Practise with me on Sundays?"

qa.a: He practised against the wall of their Mumbai building.

qa.q: What does Joseph's tight throat suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he felt disappointed and close to tears after losing.

qa.q: Which choice by Joseph showed good sportsmanship?
qa.a: He shook Zubin's hand and praised Zubin's smashes despite feeling upset.

qa.q: How does Zubin respond to Joseph's grace?
qa.a: Zubin praises Joseph's serve and invites him to practise together, showing respect.

grounding: It shows a child building skill through practice and losing gracefully.

"I saw. Your team was tired."

"Did you shake hands after?"

passage: I'm Bidisha. When I was twelve, our kabaddi team reached the district final. For weeks I'd practised my raids every evening in the school ground until my knees were scraped. In the final, Kalyani's team was faster. I got tagged out twice and we lost. I wanted to kick the mat. Instead, I lined up with everyone and shook hands. When I reached Kalyani, I said, "You were too good today." She said, "Your raid in the first half scared me." I didn't expect that. It made me want to practise even more for next year.

qa.a: Bidisha practised raids in the school ground.

passage: Coach's note, junior badminton, Saturday. Pallavi (10) reached the final of the club tournament today. For six weeks she has come early to practise her low serve against the wall, even on days her friends skipped. Today it showed: her serves were clean. She lost the final in three games to a taller girl from Andheri. At the last point she threw her head back and I saw her blinking hard. But she walked straight to the net, shook hands and said, 'Good game, your smashes were amazing.' Only after that did she sit on the bench and cry into her towel. I sat beside her and said nothing for a while. On Monday we'll look at her backhand. — Coach Himani

qa.q: What did Pallavi practise early for six weeks?
qa.a: She practised her low serve against the wall.

qa.q: What does Pallavi's blinking and later crying suggest she felt?
qa.a: She was deeply disappointed about losing but held back her tears until she had congratulated her opponent.

qa.q: Why was Coach Himani's choice to sit silently a good one?
qa.a: It let Pallavi feel her disappointment with support nearby, without rushing her or turning it into a lesson.

qa.q: How might the girl from Andheri remember the final?
qa.a: She would likely remember Pallavi as a kind, fair opponent who praised her smashes even after losing.

grounding: A coach records a child building skill through repeated practice and losing gracefully.

passage: Wednesday. Chess club tournament today. I have practised knight moves every night for a month, even the boring puzzles Uncle printed for me. I won my first two games! Then I played Afreen. She is ten, one year younger than me, and I thought it would be easy. She trapped my queen in fifteen moves. I felt like knocking all the pieces off the board. My face was so hot. But I remembered what Sir says, 'Shake hands first, feel later.' So I said 'good game' through my teeth. It came out weird. Afreen said 'good game' back and showed me where I went wrong. Actually useful. Still annoyed. Practising queen safety tomorrow. — Zubin

qa.a: Afreen trapped Zubin's queen in fifteen moves.

qa.q: How can you tell Zubin was angry after losing to Afreen?
qa.a: Zubin's face was hot, Zubin felt like knocking the pieces off the board and said 'good game' through gritted teeth.

qa.q: How might Afreen see Zubin's 'good game'?
qa.a: She may have noticed it sounded strained but still felt respected, since Zubin listened when she pointed out the mistake. 🙂

Every evening in their village near Hubli, Kavitha, ten, practised kabaddi in the dusty ground behind the school. Raid, touch, back. Raid, touch, back. Her knees were always scraped.
At the district festival, her team reached the final against Uday's team from the next village. They lost by two points.
Kavitha felt tears come. She wanted to kick the dust.
Instead she walked to Uday's team and shook hands. “Good game. Your ankle hold is really good.”
Uday grinned. “Your raids too.”
The next evening, Kavitha was back behind the school, practising the ankle hold.

At the tennis club in Buenos Aires, Hana, eleven, stayed after training every Tuesday to practise her serve. Fifty serves. Most went into the net at first.
By the club tournament, she was getting half of them in.
In the semi-final she played Valentina, who had been playing for four years. Hana lost six games to three.
She walked to the net, shook hands and said, “Your backhand is amazing.”
Valentina smiled. “Your serve is getting really good.”
Hana smiled back. On the bus home she already planned next Tuesday's fifty serves.

qa.q: How many serves did Hana practise every Tuesday?
qa.a: Fifty serves.

qa.a: She felt disappointed but proud of her progress and motivated to keep practising.

At the chess club in the community centre, Reena, twelve, had been practising openings every evening for three weeks. She had them written in a notebook.
In the final, she played Minakshi. For twenty minutes it was even. Then Reena made a mistake and lost her queen. She lost the game.
She stared at the board. Her throat tightened.
Then she held out her hand. “Well played. How did you see that move?”
Minakshi showed her. Reena wrote it in her notebook.
The club coach said, “That's how champions learn.”

qa.q: How long had Reena been practising openings?
qa.a: Every evening for three weeks.

qa.q: How did Reena feel after losing her queen and the game?
qa.a: She felt upset and disappointed, her throat tightening.

qa.q: What did Reena do after losing that shows good sportsmanship and learning?
qa.a: She shook hands, praised Minakshi and asked how she saw the move, then wrote it down.

qa.q: How might Minakshi feel when Reena asks about her move?
qa.a: She probably feels proud and respected, happy to share.

I'm Anjali, Anirban's cousin. Every evening this summer, Anirban practised his badminton serve against the wall of our building. Fifty serves. I counted once out of boredom.
At first the shuttle went everywhere. After two weeks, it hit the same brick almost every time.
Then he played the inter-colony match against a taller boy. He lost, badly. I thought he'd throw his racquet.
He didn't. He walked to the net, shook the boy's hand, and said, "Good game. Your smash is scary."
On the way home he was quiet. The next evening he was back at the wall, practising smashes.

The district badminton trial was on Saturday, and Hansa only had the school court on Tuesday and Thursday, forty minutes each, because the seniors had it the rest of the time. So she practised her backhand against the garage wall at home, hundreds of times, until the neighbour's dog stopped barking at the noise.
On Thursday it poured and the court flooded. Coach moved them into the corridor, where Hansa and Hafsa could only rally without jumping.
Saturday, they met in the second round. Hafsa won 21–17, 21–19. Hansa's eyes stung. She took a breath, walked to the net, shook Hafsa's hand properly and said, "Your drop shots got me every time."
In the car she asked Papa if they could go to the park court on Sundays.

qa.a: Hansa felt disappointed and close to tears, but she took a breath and congratulated Hafsa properly.

qa.q: What could Hansa try next to improve?
qa.a: She could practise at the park court on Sundays and work on returning drop shots, since those beat her.

Every Christmas week, the colony in Bandra held a carrom tournament under the fairy lights in the courtyard. Lalit had practised all November on the board at home, flicking the striker until his finger was sore.
He reached the final against Sangeeta, who was two years older and had won last year. He was ahead until the last board, when she pocketed the queen and cover in one shot and cleared three coins after it.
Lalit wanted to shove the board. Instead he sat on his hands for a second. Then he said, "How did you angle that queen shot?"
Sangeeta showed him, slowly, twice. The aunties clapped for both of them. Walking home, Lalit was already practising the angle in the air with his finger.

qa.a: Lalit played Sangeeta, who was two years older and had won last year.

qa.q: Why did Lalit sit on his hands for a second?
qa.a: Lalit felt frustrated and angry enough to want to shove the board, so he held himself still to calm down.

qa.q: Which choice turned the loss into practice, and why?
qa.a: Asking Sangeeta how she angled the queen shot, because it turned her win into something he could learn.

qa.q: How might Sangeeta see Lalit's question after the final?
qa.a: She might feel flattered and respect him more, since he treated her win as skill to learn from instead of luck.

"Don't talk to me." Kunal threw his muddy boots at the door. Rain was still hammering the tin roof.
"You lost one match," Shreya said. "In a flood."
"We lost 4–0! I missed the penalty!"
"You also saved two before that. I saw."
"Nobody remembers saves."
"I do." She tossed him a towel. "Did you shake their hands?"

"Hmm."
"Their goalie was really good, okay?"
"So tell him that. You'll see him at practice on Saturday."
Kunal rubbed his hair. "Can we do penalties in the lane tomorrow? You take them, I'll dive."
"In the mud?"
"It's the monsoon, Didi. It's always mud."
Shreya laughed. "Fine. Twenty each."

Last summer holidays, I practised badminton every morning at six before it got hot. I'm Arohi, and I was twelve. Coach made me do the same backhand drill fifty times a day. It was so boring I cried once.
By the colony tournament in June, my backhand actually worked. I reached the final against Vandana, who is two years older. I lost, 21–17, 21–15.
I wanted to throw my racquet. Instead, I walked to the net and shook Vandana's hand. "Your drop shots are amazing," I said. She smiled. "Your backhand was annoying. In a good way."
Back home I sulked for an hour. Then I asked Coach if I could learn drop shots next.

qa.a: Coach made Arohi do the same backhand drill fifty times a day.
